gloss: stand, take one's stand; set up, erect, fix; pillar, post
summary: To stand placed and upright, and to set up so that a thing stands. The niphal is to take one's stand for a purpose (Yahweh on the rock, the angel in Balaam's way, Yahweh standing to judge), to stand by in attendance, to stand firm (“for ever, Yahweh, your word stands fixed in the heavens”), and, as a participle, one set over others, an officer; the hiphil sets up a pillar, an altar or a heap of stones, makes the sea stand as a heap, and fixes boundaries. The nouns name what stands set up: מַצֵּבָה the standing stone, set up to Yahweh by the patriarchs and forbidden by the law; נְצִיב and מַצָּב a post, a garrison, an officer; נִצָּב the haft of a sword. Arabic naṣaba “set up, erect”, nuṣub “a stone set up and worshipped” and niṣāb “a knife's handle”, and Phoenician nṣb, mṣbt “stele”, are the same root and the same things.

words.gloss: take one's stand, stand; be set over; set up, erect, fix
words.summary: About seventy-five times, in three stems. The niphal is never plain “stand” (that is עָמַד): it is standing placed, set at a spot for a purpose or set firm, and its participle names men set over others. The hiphil is the causative, to set something up so that it stands. The hithpael “take one's stand” (הִתְיַצֵּב) belongs to the root יצב, a different spelling, and is left to that root.

stems.gloss: take one's stand, station oneself; stand by; stand upright, stand firm; be set over (participle: officer, deputy)

senses.definition: To stand placed at a particular spot for a purpose: to meet someone, to watch, to bar the way, to speak or to judge.

evidence.note: “Behold, a place by me, וְנִצַּבְתָּ עַל־הַצּוּר”: a chosen spot to stand on while the glory passes.
“Be ready in the morning … וְנִצַּבְתָּ לִי שָׁם עַל־רֹאשׁ הָהָר.”
“Go to Pharaoh in the morning … וְנִצַּבְתָּ לִקְרָאתוֹ on the bank of the river.”
“Tomorrow I will stand (נִצָּב) on the top of the hill with the rod of God in my hand.”
The donkey saw “the angel of Yahweh נִצָּב בַּדֶּרֶךְ, his drawn sword in his hand”: set across the way to bar it.
“I did not know that you stood (נִצָּב) in the way to meet me.”
Balak “standing by his burnt offering”.
“Behold, I am standing (נִצָּב) by the spring of water”: the servant waits at the well for the sign.
Moses and Aaron “standing to meet them” as they came out from Pharaoh.
When Moses went out to the tent, all the people rose “and stood (וְנִצְּבוּ) each at the door of his tent”.
Dathan and Abiram came out “standing at the door of their tents”.
The six hundred armed men of Dan “stood at the entrance of the gate”.
Samuel “standing, set over them (עֹמֵד נִצָּב עֲלֵיהֶם)”, over the company of prophets: עָמַד “stand” and נִצָּב side by side.
“On the watchtower I stand (עֹמֵד) continually by day, and at my post I am stationed (נִצָּב) every night”: the parallel is עָמַד and the place is a guard post.
Wisdom “at the head of the heights, beside the way, at the crossroads נִצָּבָה”, to call to men.
“And behold, Yahweh stood (נִצָּב) above it” and spoke the promise of the land to Jacob.
“Behold, Adonai standing (נִצָּב) on a wall made with a plumb line, a plumb line in his hand.”
“I saw Adonai standing (נִצָּב) beside the altar, and he said, Strike the capitals.”
“Yahweh takes his stand (נִצָּב) to contend, and stands (עֹמֵד) to judge the peoples”: עָמַד again the parallel.
“God stands (נִצָּב) in the congregation of El; in the midst of the אֱלֹהִים he judges.”
“He has bent his bow like an enemy, his right hand set (נִצָּב) like an adversary.”
With Psa 78:13 (hiphil) below: the waters “stood (נִצְּבוּ) like a heap”.

senses.gloss: stand by, stand in attendance; stand before
senses.definition: To stand beside or before someone as attendant, servant or worshipper, ready at hand.

evidence.note: Joseph “could not restrain himself before all who stood by him (הַנִּצָּבִים עָלָיו)”: his attendants.
Saul at Gibeah “and all his servants standing about him”.
The king said “to the runners standing about him”.
“All his servants stood by with their clothes torn.”
“All the people stand about you from morning to evening.”
“The women standing by her” at the birth of Ichabod.
“Three men standing by him.”
“I am the woman who stood (הַנִּצֶּבֶת) here with you, praying to Yahweh.”
“The queen stands (נִצְּבָה) at your right hand in gold of Ophir.”
“You stand (נִצָּבִים) today, all of you, before Yahweh your God … to enter into the covenant of Yahweh your God.”

senses.gloss: stand upright; stand firm, be fixed
senses.definition: Of a thing or a person: to stand erect, or to stand fast and unmoved.

evidence.note: “My sheaf arose (קָמָה) and also stood upright (נִצָּבָה), and your sheaves gathered round and bowed down to my sheaf.”
“For ever, Yahweh, your word stands fixed (נִצָּב) in the heavens”; the next verse, “you established the earth and it stands (וַתַּעֲמֹד).”
“Surely every man, standing firm (נִצָּב), is all vapour”: even man at his firmest is breath.
The worthless shepherd will not seek the young or heal the broken, “nor sustain the one that stands (הַנִּצָּבָה)”: the sound one, still on its feet.

senses.gloss: be set over; (participle) officer, deputy, overseer
senses.definition: With עַל: to stand set over others; the participle הַנִּצָּבִים names Solomon's district officers and the overseers of his work.

evidence.note: Boaz said “to his servant who was set over the reapers (הַנִּצָּב עַל־הַקּוֹצְרִים)”.
“Doeg the Edomite, who was set over (נִצָּב עַל) the servants of Saul.”
“Solomon had twelve נִצָּבִים over all Israel, and they provided for the king and his house.”
“Azariah son of Nathan over the נִצָּבִים.”
“Those officers provided for King Solomon … each in his month.”
“Besides Solomon's chief officers who were over the work.”
“The chief officers who were over Solomon's work, five hundred and fifty.”
“There was no king in Edom; a deputy (נִצָּב) was king.”

stems.gloss: set up, erect; make stand, set, place; fix (boundaries); set apart

senses.gloss: set up, erect (a pillar, altar, heap, monument, gates)
senses.definition: To raise something so that it stands: a standing stone, an altar, a heap of stones over a grave, a monument of victory, a city's gates.

evidence.note: “Jacob set up (וַיַּצֵּב) a pillar (מַצֵּבָה) in the place where he spoke with him, a pillar of stone, and poured a drink offering on it.”
“Jacob set up a pillar on her grave; that is the pillar of Rachel's grave to this day.”
“He set up there an altar and called it El-Elohe-Israel.”
Over Absalom in the pit “they raised a very great heap of stones”.
Absalom “had taken and set up for himself the pillar (מַצֶּבֶת) … for he said, I have no son to keep my name in remembrance”.
Saul “set up a monument (יָד) for himself” at Carmel.
David struck Hadadezer as he went “to set up his monument (יָדוֹ) at the river Euphrates”.
“They set up for themselves pillars and Asherim on every high hill.”
“Set up (הַצִּיבִי) waymarks for yourself, make yourself signposts; set your heart toward the highway … return, virgin of Israel.”
“With his youngest son he shall set up its gates”: the curse on the rebuilder of Jericho.
Hiel of Bethel “set up its gates with Segub his youngest”, according to the word of Yahweh by Joshua.

senses.definition: To set something or someone in a place, to stand there.

evidence.note: “He divided the sea and let them pass through, and made the waters stand (וַיַּצֶּב) like a heap”, as the niphal of Exo 15:8.
“As for me, in my integrity you upheld me, and set me (וַתַּצִּיבֵנִי) before your face for ever.”
“He bent his bow and set me up (וַיַּצִּיבֵנִי) as a target for the arrow.”
The wicked “set (הִצִּיבוּ) a trap; they catch men”.
The Philistines' charge for sharpening tools “and to set (וּלְהַצִּיב) the goad”: to fix its point in place.

senses.definition: To set the bounds of land or peoples so that they stand.

evidence.note: “When the Most High gave the nations their inheritance … he set (יַצֵּב) the boundaries of the peoples according to the number of the sons of Israel.”
“You have set (הִצַּבְתָּ) all the boundaries of the earth; summer and winter, you formed them.”
“Yahweh tears down the house of the proud, but he establishes (וְיַצֵּב) the boundary of the widow.”

senses.definition: To set things in a place of their own, apart from the rest.

evidence.note: “Abraham set seven ewe lambs of the flock by themselves (לְבַדְּהֶן).”
“What are these seven ewe lambs which you have set by themselves?”

stems.gloss: be set up; be fixed, determined

senses.definition: To be made to stand, set up in a place.

evidence.note: “Behold, a ladder set up (מֻצָּב) on the earth, and its top reached to heaven, and behold, the angels of God ascending and descending on it.”
Jesus to Nathanael, of Gen 28:12: “you shall see heaven opened, and the angels of God ascending and descending on the Son of man.”

senses.definition: Of what is decreed: it is settled and stands.

evidence.note: Of Nineveh: “and it is fixed (וְהֻצַּב): she is uncovered, she is carried away.” The sense is drawn from the context, and the word is uncertain.

evidence.locator: Psa.82.1, נִצָּב → ἔστη; Deu.29.9, נִצָּבִים → ἑστήκατε; Gen.18.2; Exo.7.15; 33.21; 34.2; and the hiphil Gen.33.20; 35.14, 20 → ἔστησεν; ἵστημι renders נָצַב ×20

evidence.note: Jesus quotes Psa 82:6 from the psalm that opens “God stands (ἔστη) in the congregation”: “he called them gods to whom the word of God came.”

parallels.note: Stand: set beside the niphal, which adds standing placed or set at a post.
Arise; the sheaf rose and stood upright.

words.summary: A stone set up on end, the thing the hiphil sets up (Gen 35:14). The patriarchs set them up to Yahweh, as memorials and as witnesses; the law forbids it and commands Israel to break the pillars of Canaan.

senses.definition: A stone set up as a memorial of what God said or did, a witness to a covenant, or a grave marker.

evidence.note: Jacob “took the stone that he had put under his head and set it up as a pillar, and poured oil on its top”.
“This stone which I have set up as a pillar shall be the house of God.”
“I am the God of Bethel, where you anointed a pillar, where you vowed a vow to me.”
“Jacob took a stone and raised it up as a pillar.”
“This heap is a witness, and the pillar is a witness, that I will not pass over this heap to you.”
“The pillar of Rachel's grave to this day.”
Moses built an altar under the mountain “and twelve pillars, for the twelve tribes of Israel”.
Absalom's pillar, to keep his name in remembrance.
“In that day there shall be an altar to Yahweh in the midst of the land of Egypt, and a pillar to Yahweh at its border; and it shall be for a sign and for a witness to Yahweh of hosts.”
“The sons of Israel shall dwell many days without king … without sacrifice and without pillar.”

senses.definition: A standing stone of the Canaanite worship, set beside altars and Asherim, which the law forbids and commands to be broken.

evidence.note: “You shall not set up (תָקִים) for yourself a pillar, which Yahweh your God hates.”
“You shall make no idols, nor raise up a graven image or a pillar.”
“You shall utterly break down their pillars.”
“Break down their altars, smash their pillars, cut down their Asherim.”
Judah “built for themselves high places and pillars and Asherim on every high hill”.
Jehoram “put away the pillar of Baal that his father had made”.
Jehu's men brought out “the pillars of the house of Baal and burned them”.
Hezekiah “removed the high places and broke the pillars”.
Josiah “broke the pillars and cut down the Asherim”.
“According to the goodness of his land they made good pillars.”
“He will break down their altars, he will destroy their pillars.”
“I will cut off your graven images and your pillars from among you.”
Nebuchadnezzar “shall break the pillars of Beth-shemesh in the land of Egypt”.
Of Tyre: “the pillars of your strength shall go down to the ground.”

senses.definition: What is left standing of a felled tree.

evidence.note: “As a terebinth and as an oak, whose stump (מַצֶּבֶת) remains when they are felled: the holy seed is its stump.”

evidence.locator: Gen.28.18; 31.45; 35.14, 20; Deu.7.5; 2Ki.18.4 → στήλη; στήλη renders מַצֵּבָה ×18. Not used in the New Testament.

words.summary: What is set and stands at a place: a body of soldiers posted in a land, or the officer set there; once Lot's wife, a pillar of salt.

senses.definition: A body of soldiers posted in conquered or held land, by the Philistines in Israel, by David in Aram and Edom.

evidence.note: “Jonathan struck the garrison (נְצִיב) of the Philistines that was in Geba, and the Philistines heard.”
“The hill of God, where the garrisons of the Philistines are.”
“David put garrisons in Aram of Damascus, and Aram became servants to David, bringing tribute.”
“He put garrisons in Edom; in all Edom he put garrisons.”
Jehoshaphat “set garrisons in the land of Judah and in the cities of Ephraim”.
“A garrison of the Philistines was then in Bethlehem”; the same verse at 2Sa 23:14 has מַצַּב.

senses.definition: One set over a district.

evidence.note: After the list of Solomon's twelve officers (the נִצָּבִים of 1Ki 4:7): “and one officer (וּנְצִיב אֶחָד) who was in the land.”

senses.definition: Something standing upright.

evidence.note: “His wife looked back from behind him, and she became a pillar (נְצִיב) of salt.”
“Remember Lot's wife”: Jesus draws the warning from Gen 19:26.

words.gloss: standing place; post, garrison; station, office
words.summary: The place where one stands: the priests' feet in the Jordan, a garrison's post, a man's station in office.

senses.definition: The spot where someone stood.

evidence.note: Twelve stones “from the place where the priests' feet stood firm (מִמַּצַּב רַגְלֵי הַכֹּהֲנִים)”.
Joshua set up twelve stones in the Jordan “in the place where the feet of the priests stood (מַצַּב)”.

senses.definition: A military post, and the soldiers holding it.

evidence.note: “The garrison (מַצַּב) of the Philistines went out to the pass of Michmash.”
“Come, let us go over to the garrison of the Philistines.”
“Let us go over to the garrison of these uncircumcised; perhaps Yahweh will work for us, for nothing restrains Yahweh from saving by many or by few.”
“The garrison and the raiders trembled.”
“A garrison of the Philistines was then in Bethlehem” (נְצִיב at 1Ch 11:16).

senses.definition: A man's appointed place in office.

evidence.note: To Shebna, over the house: “I will thrust you from your station (מִמַּצָּבֶךָ), and from your position (מַעֲמָדְךָ) he will pull you down”: parallel מַעֲמָד, from עָמַד.

words.summary: Once, Jdg 3:22. Arabic niṣāb is the handle of a knife, the part the blade is set into, and the Arabic verb also means to put a handle to a knife, so the word is the root's, though scripture's one use cannot fix more than “the part that follows the blade in”. The key's other two tokens (Rut 2:5–6) are the niphal participle of the verb.

senses.definition: The handle of a sword, into which the blade is set.

evidence.note: Ehud's sword: “the hilt (הַנִּצָּב) also went in after the blade (הַלַּהַב), and the fat closed over the blade.”

words.gloss: something set up: siege post; standing stone
words.summary: The hophal participle used as a noun, “what is set up”. Gen 28:12, filed under the same key, is the verb's participle.

senses.definition: A post or work set up against a besieged city.

evidence.note: Against Ariel: “I will encamp against you all around, and besiege you with a post (מֻצָּב), and raise siege works (מְצֻרֹת) against you.”

senses.definition: A stone set up, in the place name “the oak of the pillar” at Shechem.

evidence.note: Abimelech was made king “by the oak of the pillar (אֵלוֹן מֻצָּב) which is in Shechem”.
At Shechem Joshua “took a great stone and set it up there under the oak that was by the sanctuary of Yahweh”: the stone the name recalls.

words.summary: Twice, as a body of men posted: the Philistine garrison at Michmash (written מַצָּבָה), and Yahweh encamped as a guard about his house.

senses.definition: Men posted to hold or guard a place.

evidence.note: “The men of the garrison (הַמַּצָּבָה) answered Jonathan and his armour-bearer”: the garrison (מַצָּב) of 1Sa 14:11.
“I will encamp about my house as a guard (מִצָּבָה), against him who passes through and him who returns, and no oppressor shall pass over them again.”

words.summary: A town in the Shephelah of Judah. The spelling is the noun נְצִיב “post, pillar”, but scripture does not say why the town bore it; the key's other two tokens (1Ki 4:19; 1Ch 11:16) are the noun. A place, so it has no name entry.

senses.definition: A town in the lowland of Judah, listed with Keilah and Mareshah.

evidence.note: “Iphtah, Ashnah, and Nezib (וּנְצִיב), Keilah, Achzib and Mareshah.”

words.summary: Biblical Aramaic, once, of the iron in the image's feet: the quality of standing firm, as the Hebrew niphal of Psa 119:89.

senses.definition: The firm strength of iron, set against the brittleness of clay.

evidence.note: “It shall be a divided kingdom, but some of the firmness (נִצְבְּתָא) of iron shall be in it, since you saw the iron mixed with the miry clay.”
“The kingdom shall be partly strong (תַקִּיפָה) and partly broken”: the firmness of the iron is strength.

words.summary: The Peshitta's verb for planting, φυτεύω in the Greek: setting a tree or vine upright in the ground. The Hebrew never plants with this root (it uses נָטַע), but the Jewish Aramaic verb is both “put up” and “plant”, which ties the planting to the setting up.

senses.definition: To set a tree, vine or vineyard in the ground; figuratively, to plant a people or a teaching.

evidence.note: “A man, a householder, who planted (נצַב) a vineyard and set a hedge about it”, after Isa 5:2.
“A man had a fig tree planted (נצִיבָא) in his vineyard.”
In the days of Lot “they ate, they drank, they bought, they sold, they planted, they built”.
“I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth.”
“Who plants a vineyard and does not eat of its fruit?”
“Every plant (נֶצבְּתָא) which my heavenly Father has not planted (נַצבָּה) shall be uprooted.”
“Receive with meekness the implanted (נצִיבָא, ἔμφυτον) word, which is able to save your souls.”

senses.definition: To be set in the ground; of believers, to be planted together with Christ.

evidence.note: “Be uprooted and be planted (וֵאתנַצַב) in the sea.”
“If we have been planted (אֵתנצֵבנ, σύμφυτοι) with him in the likeness of his death, so shall we be also in his resurrection.”

senses.definition: Something planted.

evidence.note: “Every plant (נֶצבְּתָא, φυτεία) which my heavenly Father has not planted shall be uprooted”: said of the Pharisees.

cognates.gloss: set up, erect, raise; set up or appoint (a man) for a task; (nuṣub) a stone set up and worshipped; (naṣb) a sign set up to show the way; (niṣāb) the handle of a knife
cognates.note: The same root and the same things: the verb is the hiphil “set up”; nuṣub, the stone set up and worshipped and the stones set up round the Kaaba for sacrifice, is the מַצֵּבָה of Canaan; naṣb, the waymark, is the hiphil of Jer 31:21; “I set him up as a butt” is Lam 3:12; and niṣāb, the handle of a knife, with the fourth stem “put a handle to a knife”, is נִצָּב of Jdg 3:22. Arabic ṣ (not ḍ or ẓ) stands behind צ.

evidence.locator: Book I, p. 2799, art. نصب, نَصَبَ (n39856)
evidence.note: “He set up, put up, set upright, erected, a thing … He set up, a stone as a sign, or mark … I set, or set up, such a one as an obstacle to such a thing, or as a butt … Such a one was set up, or appointed, for …”

evidence.locator: Book I, p. 2799, art. نصب, نَصْبٌ (n39863)
evidence.note: “A sign, or mark, set up to show the way; or a standard set up … stones set up on the tops of isolated small mountains, whereby travellers are to be directed.”

evidence.locator: Book I, p. 2800, art. نصب, نُصُبٌ (n39868)
evidence.note: “What is set up and worshipped to the exclusion of … the true God … a stone that is set up and so worshipped … Certain stones which were set up around the Kaabeh … upon which victims were slain in sacrifice.”

evidence.locator: Book I, p. 2800, art. نصب, نِصَابٌ (n39871)
evidence.note: “The handle of a knife; in which the [tang] is set.”
“to put a handle to a knife”.

cognates.note: The Ugaritic verb, as the Hebrew hiphil. Ugaritic ṣ cannot tell ṣ from ṣ́, so it records no sound.

evidence.note: “nṣb part. ‘to set up’ (cf. H. n-ṣ-b Hi., Arab. naṣaba, yanṣubu)” (OCR read, which loses the dots; PDF not rendered).

cognates.gloss: (verb) erect; (nṣb, mṣbt) stele; (mṣb) stele; garrison, outpost colony
cognates.note: Phoenician and Punic use the very words: the verb of erecting a stele, mṣbt the stele (the Hebrew מַצֵּבָה), nṣb a stele (the Hebrew נְצִיב), and mṣb both a stele and a garrison (the Hebrew מַצָּב), “the garrison of Tarshish … may the men of the garrison prosper” (KAI 46).

evidence.note: “v. yiphil 1. ERECT … 2. STATION people” (OCR read).
“n.m. 1. STELE … 2. OFFERING TABLE” (OCR read).
“n.m. 1. STELE … 2. GARRISON; OUTPOST COLONY” (OCR read).
“n.f. STELE”: “Aris … erected this stele to his father” (OCR read).

cognates.note: Jewish Aramaic, in the Targums and Midrash: “put up” as the Hebrew hiphil, and “plant”, as the Peshitta. The Targum of 1Sa 13:21 renders the hiphil לְהַצִּיב of the goad by the aphel. Aramaic צ here is ṣ (Aramaic writes ṭ for ṯ̣ and ʿ or q for ṣ́).

evidence.locator: s.v. נְצַב (ch.), citing Targ. Gen. IX, 20 (h. text נטע); Targ. Y. Deut. XXXII, 50; Lev. R. s. 25 (to plant trees); Af. Targ. I Sam. XIII, 21 (h. text להציב)

cognates.note: The Syriac of the Peshitta: the planting sense, as Jewish Aramaic. Syriac ṣ, as Aramaic, stands for ṣ.

evidence.note: “plant, shoot, slip, sucker … planting … sown place, plantation”; the etymology compares Arabic naṣba.

doctrine.statement: The niphal sets Yahweh at a chosen place to act: he “stood above” the ladder to give Jacob the land (Gen 28:13), he “takes his stand to contend, and stands to judge the peoples” (Isa 3:13), he stands on the wall with a plumb line to measure Israel (Amo 7:7–8) and by the altar to strike it (Amo 9:1). In Psa 82 “God stands in the congregation of El; in the midst of the אֱלֹהִים he judges”, and he charges them, “How long will you judge unjustly … Defend the poor and fatherless”, and tells them, “I said, You are אֱלֹהִים, sons of the Most High, all of you; yet you shall die like man” (Psa 82:1–2, 6–7). Jesus quotes the psalm and explains whom it means: “he called them gods to whom the word of God came” (Jhn 10:34–35). From the verses: the אֱלֹהִים among whom God takes his stand are men, Israel's judges, mortal, who bore the title because they judged by his word; and the psalm ends looking for God himself to stand up and judge: “Arise, O God, judge the earth, for you shall inherit all the nations” (Psa 82:8), the judgment and inheritance of the earth that come in his kingdom.

Before the law Jacob set up a מַצֵּבָה to Yahweh at Bethel and anointed it, and God named himself by it: “I am the God of Bethel, where you anointed a pillar” (Gen 28:18, 22; 31:13; 35:14); a pillar witnessed the covenant with Laban (Gen 31:45, 52), and Moses set up twelve at Sinai for the tribes (Exo 24:4). Then the law said, “You shall not set up for yourself a pillar, which Yahweh your God hates” (Deu 16:22; Lev 26:1), and commanded Israel to break the pillars of Canaan (Exo 23:24; Deu 7:5; 12:3). Israel set them up again “on every high hill” (1Ki 14:23; 2Ki 17:10), and the faithful kings broke them (2Ki 18:4; 23:14). From the verses: the same act, acceptable to God before he spoke, was hateful to him once he had forbidden it; worship is acceptable only as he commands, not by what the fathers once did. Hosea foretold Israel “many days without king … without sacrifice and without pillar”, and afterward returning to “seek Yahweh their God and David their king” in the latter days (Hos 3:4–5); and Isaiah foresees “in that day” an altar to Yahweh in Egypt and a pillar to him at its border, “for a sign and for a witness”, when Egypt shall know Yahweh (Isa 19:19–21).

The Peshitta's verb of this root is “plant”, and Paul uses the picture of baptism: “all of us who were baptized into Jesus Christ were baptized into his death; we were buried with him by baptism into death, that as Christ was raised from the dead … we also should walk in newness of life; for if we have been planted (ethpeel of נצב; Greek σύμφυτοι) with him in the likeness of his death, so shall we be also in his resurrection” (Rom 6:3–5), and “if we died with Christ, we believe that we shall also live with him, knowing that Christ, being raised from the dead, dies no more” (Rom 6:8–9). From the verses: what is planted in baptism is the likeness of his death; the resurrection is still future, “we shall be”, and the life it gives is life that does not die again, as his.

Left unassigned: m.db.ac (a zero-token cross-reference listing מֻצָּב, מַצָּבָה, מַצֵּבָה, מַצֶּבֶת) and n.ep.ag (מַצָּבָה, zero tokens, filed under root מצא; matsa's note says it belongs here). Shared tokens: Rut 2:5–6 are counted under both the verb and נִצָּב (they are the niphal participle, cited under the verb); Gen 28:12 under both the hophal and מֻצָּב (cited under the verb; Jdg 9:6 and Isa 29:3 under the noun); Jos 15:43, 1Ki 4:19 and 1Ch 11:16 under both נְצִיב keys (only Jos 15:43 is the town). Left out: the root יצב (hithpael הִתְיַצֵּב “take one's stand”, and Biblical Aramaic יַצִּיב “certain, true”, Dan 2:8, 45; 3:24; 6:13; 7:16, and the pael יַצָּבָא, Dan 7:19, BDB xj.aj.*), a different spelling and its own root key; it has no entry yet and should get one, with a note on its likeness to נצב. No personal name is formed from the root (TIPNR has Nezib@Jos.15.43 as a place only). Peshitta: SEDRA root 1200 N/B, lexemes 2013 and 2014, found through the Haqor database's SEDRA word links (Mat 15:13; 21:33; Mrk 12:1; Luk 13:6; 17:6, 28; 20:9; Rom 6:5; 1Co 3:6–8; 9:7; Jas 1:21); stems read from SEDRA's form codes (form 2 taken as ethpeel for Luk 17:6 and Rom 6:5). Not followed: Akkadian. Anderson–Moser list an Akkadian naṣābu “place” (AKK008193), but Oracc's naṣābu is “suck”, and no Akkadian “set up” was found in Oracc; check CAD N/2 for naṣābu and for the naṣabātu “columns” other lexicons mention. Also not followed: DULAT for Ugaritic nṣb and any noun; Ge'ez (Dillmann, Leslau) for nṣb; Payne Smith for ܢܨܒ beyond SEDRA; CAL for Old and Imperial Aramaic nṣb “stele”. Krahmalkov and Segert are cited from the scan OCR, which writes ṣ as $ or s; page numbers by the page markers in the OCR. Open questions: (1) Nam 2:8 וְהֻצַּב is obscure (perhaps a name or a word of another root); it is kept as the hophal “it is fixed” from the context only. (2) Whether the Peshitta's “plant” should count as the root's sense on the Hebrew side: it is tied only through Jewish Aramaic “put up; plant”, and no Hebrew verse plants with נצב. (3) 1Sa 13:21 לְהַצִּיב הַדָּרְבָן: “set” the goad, or (with the Targum's aphel) “sharpen” it. (4) The doctrine statements are reasoned conclusions to review.
